1
INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
The League of Women Voters (the “League”) is a
nonprofit, nonpartisan, grassroots membership
organization committed to protecting voting rights,
empowering voters, and defending democracy.
Through advocacy, education, mobilization, and
litigation, the League works to ensure that all vote rs
have the information and opportunity to exercise their
right to vote. Founded in 1920 as an outgrowth of the
struggle to win voting rights for women, the League
now has more than one million members and
supporters in nearly 800 communities across all states
and the District of Columbia. For more than 100 years,
the League has been at the forefront of nationwide
efforts to register voters, operating one of the longestrunning and largest voter registration efforts in the
nation.
The League played a central role in shaping and
supporting the National Voter Registration Act of
1993 (“NVRA”). The League supported the NVRA’s
goal of making voter registration easier and more
accessible across the country. The League helped
spearhead the “Motor Voter” coalition to build a
grassroots campaign in favor of legislation to make
voter registration systems more accessible. President
Clinton celebrated the League and the Motor Voter
coalition as “fighters for freedom” during remarks
upon the signing of the NVRA.

1  No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in

2
Multiple League presidents provided testimony to
Congress while the NVRA was under consideration, in
part to highlight the strain that a patchwork of
outdated and inefficient registration systems across
states and localities had on the League’s mission to
register as many eligible voters as possible. In 1989,
League President Nancy M. Neuman testified,
“[O]rganizations that wish to register voters residing
in differ ent states must sort through a maze of
variable practices just to begin their work.”  Voter
Registration: Hearing Before the Subcomm. on
Elections of the Comm. on H. Admin., 101st Cong. 147
(1989). In 1993, League President Becky Cain testified
about the systemic hurdles that prevented the League
from realizing its voter registration goals: “We speak
from practical experience when we say that the
current system of voter regist ration does not and
cannot meet the needs [of] our mobile society.” Voter
Registration: Hearing Before the Subcomm. on
Elections of the Comm. on H. Admin., 103d Cong. 140
(1993).
The League also provided input and testimony to
Congress regarding list  maintenance sections of the
NVRA. The League was concerned about how
systematic purges of voter rolls near elections could
disenfranchise eligible voters and undermine the work
and mission of voter registration groups. League
President Susan S. Lederman testified about a
League-conducted nationwide survey of voter
registration laws that found “many examples of
arbitrary purging practices,” including “one
jurisdiction [where] purging [was] done in
September . . . at least in part, based on lists of
allegedly unqualified voters supplied by political

3
parties.” Hearing Before the Senate Rules Comm. on S.
250 The National Voter Registration Act, 102nd Cong.
(1991). League President Nancy Neuman’s
Congressional testimony made specific reference to a
mass purge in New York City, where the removal of
350,000 names from the rolls just before the April
1988 presidential primary negated the
accomplishments of a city -wide voter registration
drive that had added 350,000 new registrants:
“Although the League of Women Voters appreciates
the importance of maintaining the accuracy of lists of
eligible voters, it is concerned about ‘purging
procedures’ used i n many states. . . Administrative
convenience should not prevail over a basic right.”
Voter Registration: Hearing Before the Subcomm. on
election of the Comm. on H. Admin., 101st Cong. 149-
150 (1989). Early versions of the NVRA did not contain
any provisions preventing states and localities from
purging voters from their rolls in the lead up to an
election. See National Voter Registration Act of 1989,
H.R. 15 , 101st Cong. (1989). As list maintenance
provisions were added to the proposed bill, the League
and the Motor Voter Coalition brainstormed adding a
corresponding “quiet period ” during which systemic
list maintenance would be prevented.  This led to the
development of the prohibition on systematic voter
purges within 90 days of federal elections.  52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A). The insertion of this quiet period into
the NVRA assuaged the League’s concerns about
purges undermining its work registering voters and
causing confusion and chaos.

4
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
For three decades, the N VRA has done what
Congress designed it to do. It has streamlined
registration while keeping the voter rolls accurate.
Congress paired the NVRA’s registration -efficiency
and modernization provisions with list -maintenance
safeguards so that this intended balance would hold.
As a result, the NVRA remains a staple of the modern
American election system that makes voter
registration easier, more accessible, and more precise.
Petitioners now ask this Court to upset that
balance by narrowing the NVRA’s list -maintenance
protections, letting states purge voters with little
warning and less process. Congress rejected that
approach once before. Prior to the NVRA, a patchwork
of inconsistent state registration and purge practices
swept eligible voters off the rolls, even on the eve of an
election. The League of Women Voters lived that
history, and its advocacy helped persuade Congress to
replace the patchwork w ith predictable rules,
including quiet -period protections against purges
close to an election.
That legislative action rests on firm constitutional
footing. The E lections Clause gives Congress broad
authority to regulate the registration process, and
courts have consistently upheld the NVRA against
constitutional challenges in the thirty years since its
enactment.
The NVRA has worked in practice. It has driven
registration rates higher nationwide, while providing
for predictable list -maintenance rules and robust
enforcement by the federal government . The League,

5
and other advocacy organizations have  brought
successful litigation under the NVRA to stop the kind
of severely flawed mass purges that prompted
Congress to act in the first place.
Weakening the NVRA’s protections now would
invite the same chaos and disenfranchisement that led
Congress to enact the statute. The decision below
should be affirmed.
ARGUMENT
I. The NVRA was Designed to Improve
Access to the Ballot While Maintaining
Accurate Voter Rolls
In the 1990s Congress set out to address the low
turnout that plagued the elections of the 70s and 80s.
To do so, it struck a balance between streamlined
voter registration and maintenance of the voter rolls.
Because that balancing sits comfortably within
Congress’s Election s Clause authority, this Court
should not disturb it.
A. Barriers to voter registration and
aggressive purges of eligible voters
necessitated the enactment of the
NVRA
The voter registration regime of the 1970s and 80s
was characterized by a chaotic lack of uniformity.
States varied widely in what they demanded of
prospective voters and individual county and local
registrars differed widely in whether and how they
enforced those requirements. Alexander Keyssar, The
Right to Vote: The Contested History of Democracy in
the United States  253-4 (2000); Voter Registration:
Hearing Before the Subcomm. on Elections of the

6
Comm. on H. Admin.,  103d Cong. 135 (1993). The
effect of this was predictable. Contemporary estimates
suggested that restrictive  voter registration laws
reduced turnout in the 1972 presidential election by
approximately nine percentage points. Rosenstone,
Steven J., and Raymond E. Wolfinger, The Effect of
Registration Laws on Voter Turnout, 72 Am. Pol. Sci.
Rev. 22 (1978); see also National Municipal League, A
Model Election System 1 (1973) (“[T]he problem of
non-voting in America is directly related to the
machinery states have created for registering voters
and administering elections”).
This impact was further exacerbated by the
discretionary purging of eligible voters from the voter
rolls. Certain states, for instance, purged voters from
the rolls without notice merely because they failed to
vote in a previous election. See Arnold I. Menchel,
Election Laws: The Purge for Failure to Vote , 7 Conn.
L. Rev. 372, 373-78 (1975). In other states, aggressive
voter caging2 efforts led to thousands of eligible voters
having their registrations challenged in the weeks
leading up to elections. See, e.g., Democratic Nat.
Comm. v. Republican Nat. Comm ., 671 F. Supp. 2d
575, 579 (D.N.J. 2009), aff’d, 673 F.3d 192 (3d Cir.

2 Voter caging is the practice of sending mail to addresses on
the voter rolls, compiling a list of the mail that is returned
undelivered, and using that list to purge or challenge
registrations on the grounds that the voters on the list do not
legally reside at their registered addresses.  Justin Levitt, A
Guide to Voter Caging , Brennan Center ( June 29, 2007),
https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/researchreports/guide-voter-caging.

7
2012) (recounting voter caging effort in 1981) . It also
led to armed confrontations at polling sites. Id.
This history was not lost on  Congress. The
legislative record is chock-full of discussions about the
“complicated maze of local laws and procedures  . . .
which eligible citizens had to navigate in order to
exercise their right to vote,” H.R. Rep. No.  103-9, at 3
(1993), as well as the aggressive and “selective”
purging of voter rolls that forced citizens to navigate
those laws time and again. See generally  S. Rep.
No. 103-6, at 3 (1993); Voter Registration: Hearing
Before the Subcomm. on Elections of the Comm. On H.
Admin., 101st Cong. 149 (1989).
B. The NVRA’s purpose and legislative
history reflect efforts to balance
increased voter registration with
predictable, uniform list
maintenance rules
It was against that backdrop that Congress struck
a delicate balance. It expressly recognized that
“discriminatory and unfair registration laws and
procedures can have a direct and damaging effect o n
voter participation in elections for Federal office and
disproportionately harm voter participation by
various groups, including racial minorities.” And it
resolved to “assist in reducing barriers, particularly
government-imposed barriers, to applying for
registration wherever possible,” H.R. Rep. No.  103-9,
at 3, while still “[e]nsuring that expanding the
opportunities to register would in no way weaken the
validity of the registration rolls.” Id. at 5.
The N VRA, accordingly, did just that. Its stated
goals were twofold. First, to establish procedures that

8
would increase the number of citizens who register
and vote. 52 U.S.C. §  20501(b)(1)-(2). And second, it
sought to maintain accurate voter rolls and a secure
election process while doing so. 52 U.S.C.
§ 20501(b)(3)-(4). To achieve its first objective, the
NVRA established a streamlined voter registration
process, including a uniform federal form and
opportunities to register through motor -vehicle
agencies and by mail. 52 U.S.C. § 20504-5. To achieve
the second —while avoiding the aggressive purging
that had r outinely knocked eligible voters from the
rolls prior to its enactment —the NVRA prescribed
safeguards that states must follow as they monitor the
accuracy of their voter rolls. A state must, for instance,
make a reasonable effort to remove the names of
voters who have died or moved. 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(a)(4). At the same time, a state must not
systematically remove ineligible voters from the rolls
within 90  days of an election. 52 U.S.C.
§ 20507(c)(2)(A).
The new interpretation of this 90 -day provision
advanced by Petitioners and the United States —that
it does not apply to removals based on suspected lack
of citizenship—cannot be reconciled with the NVRA’s
legislative history. Congress explained that the 90-day
quiet period applies to any systematic program to
“confirm voting lists.” H.R. Rep. No.  103-66, at 20.
Including removals on grounds other than suspected
change in residence or death. H.R. Rep. No. 103-9, at
16 (noting that the 90 -day provision would apply to
canvassing efforts). Accordingly, the provision, while
limited in time, is sweeping in scope . Its text reflects
that breadth. It bars “any program” that

9
systematically removes ineligible voters from the list
of eligible voters. 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A).
This approach is reasonable  and true to the
statutory text, particularly when viewed in light of its
historical context and purpose. The 90-day provision
permits the continuing removal of ineligible voters
based on individualized inquiries  while protecting
eligible voters from being swept up in systematic
purges without sufficient time to reregister. See Arcia
v. Fla. Sec ’y of State , 772 F.3d 1335, 1346 (11th Cir.
2014) (“Eligible voters removed days or weeks before
Election Day will likely not be able to correct the
State's errors in time to vote.”). It would blow a hole in
the provision to allow systematic removals  for any
reason, including suspected lack of citizenship ,
because such purges can —and do—sweep in eligible
voters just as easily as systematic removals based on
suspected change of residence or death. A fact that has
been borne out in Arcia and more than a decade of
subsequent litigation. See, e.g., Fish v. Kobach, 840
F.3d 710 (10th Cir. 2016); Va. Coal. for Immigrant Rts.
v. Beals, 803 F. Supp. 3d 454, 461 (E.D. Va. 2025) ;
LULAC v. Whitley, No. SA -19-CA-074-FB, 2019 WL
7938511 (W.D. Tex. Feb. 27, 2019).
Since long before  the NVRA’s enactment, states
have raised concerns about inaccurate voter rolls and
fraud. But then, as now, the League and others
explained the impact of aggressive purging and
needless and demanding registration requirements on
eligible voters. The NVRA balanc ed both of those
concerns consistent with Congress’s authority under
the Elections Clause.

10
C. The NVRA has a strong
constitutional basis
While the Elections Clause gives states the initial
authority to regulate the time, place, and manner of
elections, it vests in Congress supervisory authority to
alter those regulations or supplant them altogether.
Art. 1 §  4, Cl. 1; U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton ,
514 U.S. 779, 804-805 (1995). Congress’s power under
the E lections Clause is, at its core, the power to
preempt. Thus, when it legislates pursuant to this
authority “it necessarily displaces some element of a
pre-existing legal regime erected by the States.”
Arizona v. Inter  Tribal Council of Arizona, Inc. , 570
U.S. 1, 14 (2013). The scope of this power is broad, a s
James Madison explained, the clause employs “words
of great latitude.” 2 RECORDS OF THE FEDERAL
CONVENTION OF 1787 at 240. Accordingly, this
Court has long understood that supervisory authority
to extend to regulations related to “registration.” See
Smiley v. Holm , 285 U.S. 355, 366 (1932); Ex parte
Siebold, 100 U.S. 371 (1879). It is little surpr ise,
therefore, that courts rejected constitutional
challenges to the NVRA following its enactment. See,
e.g., Ass’n of Cmty. Organizations for Reform Now
(ACORN) v. Edgar, 56 F.3d 791 (7th Cir. 1995); Voting
Rts. Coal. v. Wilson, 60 F.3d 1411 (9th Cir. 1995); Ass’n
of Cmty. Organizations for Reform Now v. Miller , 129
F.3d 833 (6th Cir. 1997). This strong constitutional
footing has ensured the NVRA’s lasting impact.

11
II. The NVRA has Successfully Balanced the
Goals of Improving Access to the Ballot
with the Need for Accurate Voter Rolls
and List Maintenance
Data confirms that the NVRA has effectively
fulfilled it s purposes as set forth by Congress. In
1995—the year in which most states implemented the
NVRA—the Federal Election Commission (“FEC”)
reported that states covered by the NVRA saw a total
of 41,452,428 voter registration applications. Out of
those applications, a significant percentage came from
sources that the League championed, including 13.7
million in registration at motor vehicle offices, 12.3
million in registration b y mail, and another 10.8
million from organized registration drives, deputy
registrars, and in -person registrations. Fed. Election
Comm’n, The Impact of the National Voter
Registration Act of 1993 on the Administration of
Elections for Federal Office 1995-1996, at 12-13 (1997).
In total, the new avenues of voter registration created
by the NVRA accounted for more than 30.6 million
voter registration applications and registration
updates.
Data shows that the NVRA has helped make voter
registration easier for eligible U.S. citizens over the
years. Upon its enactment, the percentage of
registered voters was estimated to be around sixty to
sixty-one percent of eligible voters. See H.R. Rep.
No. 103-9, at 3 (1993), (citing Congressional Research
Service figures showing “only slightly over 60 percent
of the eligible voters are registered”); S. Rep. No. 103-
6, at 2 (1993) (citing Congressional Research Service
figures showing “only approximately 61 percent of

12
those eligible to vote are registered”). Since then, the
Election Assistance Commission’s (“EAC”) Election
Administration and Voting Survey (EAVS) has
tracked a rise in the registration rate of the citizen
voting age population from 73.6% in 2006 to 87.5% in
2024. U.S. Election Assistance Comm’n, EAVS Data
Interactive (last updated Sept. 10, 2026),
https://www.eac.gov/research-and-data/studies-andreports/eavs-data-interactive (last visited Oct. 15,
2026). As registration has grown more accessible
across the country, the League and its state and local
affiliates have registered more than 1.5 million voters
nationwide since 2016.
Along with expanding access to voter registration,
the NVRA has achieved its other goals: providing
states with predictable guidelines to conduct list
maintenance, while limiting the severe impact of
flawed voter purges. An integral part of achieving the
balance that the NVRA sought has been the successful
enforcement efforts by the federal government and
private organizations, including the League. These
enforcement efforts have prevented the chaos or
remedied the harm of voter purges close to the election
that Congress sought to address. See e.g., Ala. Coal.
for Immigrant Justice  v. Allen , 2:24-CV-1254-AMM,
2024 WL 4510476 (N.D. Ala. Oct. 16, 2024) (enjoining
Alabama’s purge of 3,251 voters eighty -four days
before the November 2024 election); Stipulation of
Facts and Consent Order, United States v. Bd. of
Election Comm’rs for St. Louis , No.  4:02-cv-01235
(E.D. Mo. Aug. 14, 2002), ECF No.  4. (consent decree
stipulating to revised list maintenance procedures
after the City of St. Louis had removed 54,000 voters
from the rolls without proper notice, causing the

13
Board of Elections downtown office to be overwhelmed
on Election Day as voters attempted to remedy their
registration).
In sum, the voter registration environment under
the NVRA resembles the well -balanced system
Congress intended: widespread, increasing access to
voter registration, regularized list maintenance, and
robust enforcement from public and private actors.
III. Removing the NVRA’s Protections Against
Voter Purges Would Spur Litigation and
Disenfranchisement
The NVRA’s 90 -day quiet period is essential to
preventing disenfranchisement of eligible and lawful
voters. Weakening the NVRA would be felt across a
wide range of voters, including low-income voters of all
races and backgrounds who lack documentary proof of
citizenship, women who have cha nged their name
after marriage, rural voters without easy access to
elections and other governmental offices, and recently
naturalized citizens. Ian Vandewalker, Brennan Ctr.
for Just., The Effects of Requiring Documentary Proof
of Citizenship to Register to Vote  (July 19, 2017).
Gutting these protections would inevitably increase,
not decrease, election litigation. The League knows
this well. It has relied on these provisions to prevent
the disenfranchisement of Alabama, Georgia, and
Kansas voters who lacked readily available proof of
citizenship, and it continues to do s o. See Fish v.
Kobach, 840 F.3d 710 (10th Cir. 2016); LWV v. Newby,
838 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir . 2016). Were the NVRA’s
protections and rules to fall away, courts would be
forced to wade into murkier constitutional waters,
including through eleventh -hour litigation in the

14
middle of ongoing elections. See, e.g.,  Anderson v.
Celebrezze, 460 U.S. 780 (1983) ; Burdick v. Takushi ,
504 U.S. 428 (1992); Va. Coal. for Immigrant Rts . v.
Beals, No.  24-2071, 2024 WL 4601052 (4th Cir. Oct.
27, 2024), stayed, 2024 WL 4608863 (U.S. Oct 30,
2024). See also People Not Politicians v. Onder ,
26A388, 2026 WL 2883222 (U.S. Sept. 25, 2026);
Republican Nat’l. Comm. v. Democratic Nat’l. Comm.,
589 U.S. 42 4 (2020) (“This Court has repeatedly
emphasized that lower federal courts should
ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an
election. See Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1 (2006) (per
curiam).”). The E lections Clause was designed
precisely to allow Congress to prevent such chaos.
Through the NVRA, it has done so.
CONCLUSION
The decision below should be affirmed.
